§ Simple Magnetic Circuit

For a really high μ\muμ: magnetic flux will be confined to the paths defined by the structure. Thus, we can use magnetic circuit to simplify this model.

Details:

  • The source of MF (InetI_{net}Inet​), F=N⋅i\mathscr{F} = N \cdot iF=N⋅i we call F\mathscr{F}F as magnetomotive force (mmf) For multiple windings: F=N1⋅i1+N2⋅i2+⋯\mathscr{F} = N_1 \cdot i_1 + N_2 \cdot i_2 + \cdotsF=N1​⋅i1​+N2​⋅i2​+⋯
  • Magnetic flux: ϕ=∫sB⃗⋅da⃗\phi = \int_s \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{a}ϕ=∫s​B⋅da (Wb) Simplify as MC: ϕc=Bc⋅Ac\phi_c = B_c \cdot A_cϕc​=Bc​⋅Ac​ϕc\phi_cϕc​: core flux, BcB_cBc​: core flux density
  • mmf: According to Ampere's Law: F=Inet=∮H⃗⋅dl⃗\mathscr{F} = I_{net} = \oint \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l}F=Inet​=∮H⋅dl For MC: H⃗≈H⃗c\vec{H} \approx \vec{H}_cH≈Hc​, l≈lcl \approx l_cl≈lc​, so: F=N⋅i=Hc⋅lc\mathscr{F} = N \cdot i = H_c \cdot l_cF=N⋅i=Hc​⋅lc​ ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ Hc=NilcH_c = \frac{Ni}{l_c}Hc​=lc​Ni​
  • H⃗\vec{H}H & B⃗\vec{B}B: B⃗=μH⃗⇒B=μNilc\vec{B} = \mu\vec{H} \Rightarrow B = \mu \frac{Ni}{l_c}B=μH⇒B=μlc​Ni​

ϕc=BcAc=μNilcAc\phi_c = B_c A_c = \mu \frac{Ni}{l_c} A_cϕc​=Bc​Ac​=μlc​Ni​Ac​ ∼\sim∼ I=J⋅aI = J \cdot aI=J⋅a

Magnetic analogue to Kirchhoff's Law:

Divergence of B⃗=0\vec{B} = 0B=0 (∇⋅B⃗=0\nabla \cdot \vec{B} = 0∇⋅B=0)

Total flux entering one node is 0.

Reluctance of MC: Series: R=R1+R2+R3+⋯\mathscr{R} = \mathscr{R}_1 + \mathscr{R}_2 + \mathscr{R}_3 + \cdotsR=R1​+R2​+R3​+⋯ Parallel: 1R=1R1+1R2+1R3+⋯\frac{1}{\mathscr{R}} = \frac{1}{\mathscr{R}_1} + \frac{1}{\mathscr{R}_2} + \frac{1}{\mathscr{R}_3} + \cdotsR1​=R1​1​+R2​1​+R3​1​+⋯

The errors in MC computation:

  • There is a small fraction of the flux escapes from the core into the air. The flux outside is called leakage flux.
  • The assumption of l=lcl = l_cl=lc​ is not really very good, especially at corners.
  • In ferromagnetic materials, the μ\muμ varies with the amount of flux already inside. Thus, the effect is always nonlinear.
  • Air gap "fringing effect".

§ Magnetic Circuit with Air Gap

Provided ggg is sufficiently small, we can analyze this as two series components.

Ignoring the leakage: ϕc=ϕg=ϕ\phi_c = \phi_g = \phiϕc​=ϕg​=ϕ

F=Ni=∮H⃗⋅dl⃗=Hclc+Hgg=Bcμlc+Bgμ0g\mathscr{F} = Ni = \oint \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l}= H_c l_c + H_g g = \frac{B_c}{\mu} l_c + \frac{B_g}{\mu_0} gF=Ni=∮H⋅dl=Hc​lc​+Hg​g=μBc​​lc​+μ0​Bg​​g

⇒\Rightarrow⇒ F=ϕ(lcμAc+gμ0Ag)\mathscr{F} = \phi (\frac{l_c}{\mu A_c} + \frac{g}{\mu_0 A_g})F=ϕ(μAc​lc​​+μ0​Ag​g​)

⇒\Rightarrow⇒ verify the R\mathscr{R}R series' law:

R=Rc+Rg=lcμAc+gμ0Ag\mathscr{R} = \mathscr{R}_c + \mathscr{R}_g = \frac{l_c}{\mu A_c} + \frac{g}{\mu_0 A_g}R=Rc​+Rg​=μAc​lc​​+μ0​Ag​g​

As μ\muμ is relatively much higher than μ0\mu_0μ0​ (2000∼800002000 \sim 800002000∼80000 times), Rg≫Rc\mathscr{R}_g \gg \mathscr{R}_cRg​≫Rc​

R≈Rg\mathscr{R} \approx \mathscr{R}_gR≈Rg​, ϕ≈Niμ0Agg\phi \approx Ni \frac{\mu_0 A_g}{g}ϕ≈Nigμ0​Ag​​

As we mentioned before, μ\muμ in the core will change with flux inside. But with ϕ≈Niμ0Agg\phi \approx Ni \frac{\mu_0 A_g}{g}ϕ≈Nigμ0​Ag​​, its variation won't significantly affect the performance of MC, because the dominant R\mathscr{R}R is that in air gap.

☆ Fringing effect: why Ag≠AcA_g \neq A_cAg​=Ac​?

The fringing effect causes AgA_gAg​ to increase, so there is always Ag>AcA_g > A_cAg​>Ac​. If fringing is neglected, Ag=AcA_g = A_cAg​=Ac​.

§ Magnetic behavior of ferromagnetic materials

  • Saturation
ϕ=NiμAl\phi = Ni \frac{\mu A}{l}ϕ=NilμA​B=μHB = \mu HB=μH
F=Ni↑,μ↓\mathscr{F} = Ni \uparrow, \mu \downarrowF=Ni↑,μ↓H=Nil↑,μ↓H = \frac{Ni}{l} \uparrow, \mu \downarrowH=lNi​↑,μ↓

Saturation occurs when all the magnetic domains in a material are all aligned together. When the temperature reaches Curie Point (TcT_cTc​), the domains will be reoriented and μ\muμ will decrease sharply.

At first, H↑→B↑↑,μr↑H \uparrow \rightarrow B \uparrow \uparrow, \mu_r \uparrowH↑→B↑↑,μr​↑;

Then, most of domains lined up, μr\mu_rμr​ saturate as μrmax⁡\mu_{r \max}μrmax​;

Finally, H↑↑→B↑,μr↓H \uparrow \uparrow \rightarrow B \uparrow, \mu_r \downarrowH↑↑→B↑,μr​↓, no more domains can contribute to the increase of B,μ→μ0,μr→1B, \mu \rightarrow \mu_0, \mu_r \rightarrow 1B,μ→μ0​,μr​→1.

Energy loss in ferromagnetic core

Hysteresis Loss

When a ferromagnetic material is subjected into an alternating MF, BBB always lags behind HHH, which is called Hysteresis.

Root causes:

  1. Friction of domain rotation;
  2. Domain wall pinning (impurities, …\dots…); These effects above cause the process of magnetization to be irreversible. When HHH removed, some domains stay aligned, creating Remanence.

The effect of mmf on the loop

As F=Ni\mathscr{F} = NiF=Ni increasing, the loop grows taller and wider to reach the saturation point. This means hysteresis loss is higher as it equals to the area of the loop.

How to calculate Hysteresis Loss?

W=Aclm∫one cycleHdBW = A_c l_m \int_{\text{one cycle}} H dBW=Ac​lm​∫one cycle​HdB

AcA_cAc​: cross-section area

lml_mlm​: mean magnetic path length

Aclm=Volume of the coreA_c l_m = \text{Volume of the core}Ac​lm​=Volume of the core

The integral is the area of B-H Loop.

Proof: W=∫v(t)i(t)dtW = \int v(t)i(t)dtW=∫v(t)i(t)dt

Faraday's Law: v(t)=NdΦdt=NAcdB(t)dtv(t) = N \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = N A_c \frac{dB(t)}{dt}v(t)=NdtdΦ​=NAc​dtdB(t)​

Ampere's Law: H(t)lm=Ni(t)=FH(t) l_m = N i(t) = \mathscr{F}H(t)lm​=Ni(t)=F

Thus, W=Aclm∫one cycleHdBW = A_c l_m \int_{\text{one cycle}} H dBW=Ac​lm​∫one cycle​HdB is proved.

Then, as for the power: P=f⋅Aclm∫one cycleHdBP = f \cdot A_c l_m \int_{\text{one cycle}} H dBP=f⋅Ac​lm​∫one cycle​HdB

II. Transformers

Types and construction

  • Core-form: consists a simple rectangular laminated piece of steel with the transformers windings wrapped around two sides.
  • Shell-form: consists three legs laminated core with winding wrapped around the center leg.
  • Primary winding or input winding: The winding connected to the power source.
  • Secondary winding or output winding: The winding connected to the loads.
  • Core material and eddy current: The core is constructed of thin laminations electrically isolated from each other in order to minimize the eddy current.
  • Eddy current:

§ Ideal Transformer

  • Assumptions

    Neglect: Leakage flux, copper losses, hysteresis losses, eddy-current losses.

  • Characteristics

vp(t)vs(t)=NpNs=a\frac{v_p(t)}{v_s(t)} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} = avs​(t)vp​(t)​=Ns​Np​​=a

ip(t)is(t)=NsNp=1a\frac{i_p(t)}{i_s(t)} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{1}{a}is​(t)ip​(t)​=Np​Ns​​=a1​

V˙pV˙s=a\frac{\dot{V}_p}{\dot{V}_s} = aV˙s​V˙p​​=a, I˙pI˙s=1a\frac{\dot{I}_p}{\dot{I}_s} = \frac{1}{a}I˙s​I˙p​​=a1​

The turns ratio aaa only effects the magnitude not the angle.

  • Dot convention

    If the primary current flows into the dotted end of the primary winding, the secondary current will flow out of the dotted end of the secondary winding.

  • Power

    Pin=VpIpcos⁡θpP_{in} = V_p I_p \cos\theta_pPin​=Vp​Ip​cosθp​, Pout=VsIscos⁡θsP_{out} = V_s I_s \cos\theta_sPout​=Vs​Is​cosθs​

    Since the transformer can't change the angles, the primary and secondary windings have the same power factor.

    Power, reactive power, apparent power are all the same for input and output.

    Pin=PoutP_{in} = P_{out}Pin​=Pout​, Qin=QoutQ_{in} = Q_{out}Qin​=Qout​, Sin=SoutS_{in} = S_{out}Sin​=Sout​

V˙p=aV˙s\dot{V}_p = a \dot{V}_sV˙p​=aV˙s​

I˙p=1aI˙s\dot{I}_p = \frac{1}{a} \dot{I}_sI˙p​=a1​I˙s​

§ Theory of operation of real single-phase transformers

Secondary side open

  • Secondary side is open circuit.
  • Input voltage and current to measure hysteresis curve.
  • Flux is proportional to vpv_pvp​ and mmf is proportional to ipi_pip​.
  • ip(t)=0i_p(t) = 0ip​(t)=0 for ideal transformer.

Magnetization current in real transformers

  1. The magnetization current imi_mim​ is used to generate mutual flux ϕM\phi_MϕM​.
  2. While secondary side is opened, the current measured at primary side contains two parts and is called excitation current iexi_{ex}iex​, which includes:

  • Magnetization current imi_mim​:

    To generate mutual flux.

  • Core loss current ih+ei_{h+e}ih+e​:

    Hysteresis and eddy current.

  • The magnetization current in the transformer is not sinusoidal.

    The higher-frequency components are due to magnetic saturation. (i↑↑⇒ϕ↑→i \uparrow \uparrow \Rightarrow \phi \uparrow \rightarrowi↑↑⇒ϕ↑→)

  • The fundamental component of imi_mim​ lags the voltage applied to the core by 90∘90^\circ90∘.

Core-loss current

  • The core-loss current ih+ei_{h+e}ih+e​ is nonlinear because of the nonlinear effects of hysteresis.
  • The fundamental component of ih+ei_{h+e}ih+e​ is in phase with the voltage applied to the core.

Excitation current We have iex=im+ih+ei_{ex} = i_m + i_{h+e}iex​=im​+ih+e​, thus:

§ The equivalent circuit of non-ideal transformers

1> Copper losses. (I2RI^2RI2R, heating losses on windings) 2> Eddy current losses. (heating losses in the core) 3> Hysteresis losses. 4> Leakage flux. (self-inductance)

Modeling excitation current & copper losses

  • The hysteresis and eddy current is in-phase with input voltage.

    ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ Modeled as a shunt resistor RcR_cRc​.

  • The magnetization current is lagging input voltage by 90∘90^\circ90∘.

    ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ Modeled as a shunt inductor XmX_mXm​.

  • The copper loss can be modeled as series resistor RpR_pRp​ and RsR_sRs​.

§ Transformer voltage regulation and efficiency

Because a real transformer has series impedances within it, the load can influence the output voltage.

To conveniently compare transformers in this respect, we defined a quantity called voltage regulation (VR).

It's defined by the equation:

VR=Vs,nl−Vs,flVs,fl×100%VR = \frac{V_{s,nl} - V_{s,fl}}{V_{s,fl}} \times 100\% VR=Vs,fl​Vs,nl​−Vs,fl​​×100%

Vs,nlV_{s,nl}Vs,nl​: No-load voltage of secondary side

Since at no load, Vs=Vp/aV_s = V_p / aVs​=Vp​/a, thus:

VR=Vp/a−Vs,flVs,fl×100%VR = \frac{V_p/a - V_{s,fl}}{V_{s,fl}} \times 100\% VR=Vs,fl​Vp​/a−Vs,fl​​×100%

§ Transformer Phasor Diagram

To obtain the voltage regulation (VR), we use the phasor relation:

V⃗pa=V⃗s+ReqI⃗s+jXeqI⃗s\frac{\vec{V}_p}{a} = \vec{V}_s + R_{eq}\vec{I}_s + j X_{eq}\vec{I}_s aVp​​=Vs​+Req​Is​+jXeq​Is​

Phasor diagrams under different load conditions:

  • Lagging power factor (inductive load):I⃗s\vec{I}_sIs​ lags V⃗s\vec{V}_sVs​. The required primary voltage Vpa\frac{V_p}{a}aVp​​ is significantly larger than the secondary terminal voltage VsV_sVs​.

  • Unity power factor (resistive load):I⃗s\vec{I}_sIs​ is in phase with V⃗s\vec{V}_sVs​. The voltage regulation is positive but smaller than the lagging case.

  • Leading power factor (capacitive load):I⃗s\vec{I}_sIs​ leads V⃗s\vec{V}_sVs​. The terminal voltage VsV_sVs​ can actually be larger than the referred primary voltage Vpa\frac{V_p}{a}aVp​​, resulting in a negative voltage regulation.

§ Transformer Efficiency

The efficiency of a transformer is defined as:

η=PoutPin×100%=PoutPout+Ploss×100%\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\% = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{out} + P_{loss}} \times 100\% η=Pin​Pout​​×100%=Pout​+Ploss​Pout​​×100%

When is the efficiency maximized?

η=1−∑PP2+∑P\eta = 1 - \frac{\sum P}{P_{2} + \sum P} η=1−P2​+∑P∑P​

P2=U2I2cos⁡φ2≈U2NI2cos⁡φ2P_2 = U_2 I_2 \cos \varphi_2 \approx U_{2N} I_2 \cos \varphi_2 P2​=U2​I2​cosφ2​≈U2N​I2​cosφ2​

=βSNcos⁡φ2= \beta S_N \cos \varphi_2 =βSN​cosφ2​

SNS_NSN​ : Apparent Power , $S_N = U_{2N} I_{2N} $$ \beta :LoadFactor,: Load Factor ,:LoadFactor, \beta = I_2 / I_{2N} $

$P_{Fe} \approx p_0 \text{ (constance)} $$ P_{cu} = P_k = \frac{I_2^2}{I_{2N}^2} P_{kN} = \beta^2 P_{kN} $

Thus ,

η=(1−P0+β2PkNβSNcos⁡φ2+P0+β2PkN)×100%\eta = \left( 1 - \frac{P_0 + \beta^2 P_{kN}}{\beta S_N \cos \varphi_2 + P_0 + \beta^2 P_{kN}} \right) \times 100 \% η=(1−βSN​cosφ2​+P0​+β2PkN​P0​+β2PkN​​)×100%

For constant power factor :

P0=βm2PkNP_0 = \beta_m^2 P_{kN}P0​=βm2​PkN​ ，βm=P0PkN\beta_m = \sqrt{\frac{P_0}{P_{kN}}}βm​=PkN​P0​​​

β=I1I1N=I2I2N\beta = \frac{I_1}{I_{1N}} = \frac{I_2}{I_{2N}}β=I1N​I1​​=I2N​I2​​

For a certain P2NP_{2N}P2N​

we have:

1η=βP2N+P0+β2PkNβP2N=1+1P2N(P0β+βPkN)\frac{1}{\eta} = \frac{\beta P_{2N} + P_0 + \beta^2 P_{kN}}{\beta P_{2N}} = 1 + \frac{1}{P_{2N}} \left( \frac{P_0}{\beta} + \beta P_{kN} \right) η1​=βP2N​βP2N​+P0​+β2PkN​​=1+P2N​1​(βP0​​+βPkN​)

Therefore , when β=βm\beta = \beta_mβ=βm​ , (1η)min⇒ηmax\left( \frac{1}{\eta} \right)_{min} \Rightarrow \eta_{max}(η1​)min​⇒ηmax​

Efficiency is optimized when copper loss = core loss !

Core loss is constant (PFeP_{Fe}PFe​), while copper loss varies as β2PCu,fl\beta^2 P_{Cu,fl}β2PCu,fl​.

Efficiency is optimized (maximized) when copper loss equals core loss:

β2PCu,fl=PFe\beta^2 P_{Cu,fl} = P_{Fe} β2PCu,fl​=PFe​

The load factor for maximum efficiency is:

βm=PFePCu,fl\beta_m = \sqrt{\frac{P_{Fe}}{P_{Cu,fl}}} βm​=PCu,fl​PFe​​​

§ Transformer Taps and Voltage Regulation

  • Transformer Taps: Taps are intermediate connection points on the transformer windings used to change the effective turns ratio aaa. When the utility line voltage fluctuates, changing the taps helps maintain a stable output voltage.
  • TCUL (Tap Changing Under Load): A specialized transformer capable of changing its tap connections while the power is connected and the transformer is under load.
  • Voltage Regulator: A TCUL equipped with automatic voltage sensing circuitry that changes taps dynamically to maintain the output voltage at a predefined level.

§ The Autotransformer

  • Autotransformer: A transformer in which the primary and secondary windings share a common physical winding.
    • Allows continuous tuning of the output voltage magnitude.
    • The physical size (and cost) of an autotransformer is smaller than a conventional two-winding transformer of the same power rating.
    • There is no electrical isolation between the primary and secondary sides.

The Step-Up Connection of Autotransformer (AT):

An autotransformer has one continuous winding divided into:

  • Common winding with NCN_CNC​ turns.
  • Series winding with NSEN_{SE}NSE​ turns.

§ The Step-Down Connection of Autotransformer

Voltage and current relations in the windings:

  • Coil voltage and current in NCN_CNC​ and NSEN_{SE}NSE​ follow the standard transformer relations:

    VCVSE=NCNSE\frac{V_C}{V_{SE}} = \frac{N_C}{N_{SE}} VSE​VC​​=NSE​NC​​

    NCIC=NSEISEN_C I_C = N_{SE} I_{SE} NC​IC​=NSE​ISE​

  • Terminal voltage and current relationships (Step-Down):

    • Low-voltage side: VL=VCV_L = V_CVL​=VC​, IL=IC+ISEI_L = I_C + I_{SE}IL​=IC​+ISE​
    • High-voltage side: VH=VC+VSEV_H = V_C + V_{SE}VH​=VC​+VSE​, IH=ISEI_H = I_{SE}IH​=ISE​

    VLVH=NCNC+NSE\frac{V_L}{V_H} = \frac{N_C}{N_C + N_{SE}} VH​VL​​=NC​+NSE​NC​​

    ILIH=NC+NSENC\frac{I_L}{I_H} = \frac{N_C + N_{SE}}{N_C} IH​IL​​=NC​NC​+NSE​​

§ Apparatus Power Rating Advantage of Autotransformer

We define two power ratings:

  • Terminal apparent power rating (SIOS_{IO}SIO​): The apparent power transformed and delivered between terminals.

    SIO=VLIL=VHIHS_{IO} = V_L I_L = V_H I_H SIO​=VL​IL​=VH​IH​

  • Winding apparent power rating (SWS_WSW​): The actual physical capacity of the winding/core.

    SW=VCIC=VSEISES_W = V_C I_C = V_{SE} I_{SE} SW​=VC​IC​=VSE​ISE​

The relation between them is:

SW=VL(IL−IH)=SIO(1−NCNC+NSE)=SIONSENC+NSES_W = V_L (I_L - I_H) = S_{IO} \left(1 - \frac{N_C}{N_C + N_{SE}}\right) = S_{IO} \frac{N_{SE}}{N_C + N_{SE}} SW​=VL​(IL​−IH​)=SIO​(1−NC​+NSE​NC​​)=SIO​NC​+NSE​NSE​​

Therefore:

SIOSW=NC+NSENSE>1\frac{S_{IO}}{S_W} = \frac{N_C + N_{SE}}{N_{SE}} > 1 SW​SIO​​=NSE​NC​+NSE​​>1

  • Advantage: Since NC+NSE>NSEN_C + N_{SE} > N_{SE}NC​+NSE​>NSE​, the terminal capacity SIOS_{IO}SIO​ is always larger than the physical winding capacity SWS_WSW​. This advantage becomes very large when the primary and secondary voltages are close (i.e., NSEN_{SE}NSE​ is small). It provides a highly compact and inexpensive way to tie two nearly equal voltages together.

§ Review of Three-Phase Power

Three-phase systems have two main connection types: Wye (Y\text{Y}Y) and Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ).

  • Line voltage (VLV_LVL​): The voltage between any two line conductors (VABV_{AB}VAB​, VBCV_{BC}VBC​, VCAV_{CA}VCA​).

  • Phase voltage (VϕV_\phiVϕ​): The voltage across a single phase winding (VANV_{AN}VAN​, VBNV_{BN}VBN​, VCNV_{CN}VCN​).

Wye (Y\text{Y}Y) connection:

  • Line voltage is 3\sqrt{3}3​ times phase voltage: VL=3VϕV_L = \sqrt{3} V_\phiVL​=3​Vϕ​

  • Line current equals phase current: IL=IϕI_L = I_\phiIL​=Iϕ​

  • Line voltages lead their corresponding phase voltages by 30∘30^\circ30∘ (for positive sequence ABC).

Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ) connection:

  • Line voltage equals phase voltage: VL=VϕV_L = V_\phiVL​=Vϕ​

  • Line current is 3\sqrt{3}3​ times phase current: IL=3IϕI_L = \sqrt{3} I_\phiIL​=3​Iϕ​

  • Line currents lag their corresponding phase currents by 30∘30^\circ30∘ (for positive sequence ABC).

§ Three-Phase Power Equations

  • Power on a single phase:

    Pϕ=VϕIϕcos⁡θP_\phi = V_\phi I_\phi \cos\theta Pϕ​=Vϕ​Iϕ​cosθ

  • Total active power (PPP):

    P=3Pϕ=3VϕIϕcos⁡θ=3VLILcos⁡θ(W)P = 3 P_\phi = 3 V_\phi I_\phi \cos\theta = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \cos\theta \quad (\text{W}) P=3Pϕ​=3Vϕ​Iϕ​cosθ=3​VL​IL​cosθ(W)

  • Total reactive power (QQQ):

    Q=3VLILsin⁡θ(var)Q = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \sin\theta \quad (\text{var}) Q=3​VL​IL​sinθ(var)

  • Total apparent power (SSS):

    S=3VLIL(VA)S = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \quad (\text{VA}) S=3​VL​IL​(VA)

  • Phase sequence:

    • Positive sequence: A→B→CA \to B \to CA→B→C
    • Negative sequence: A→C→BA \to C \to BA→C→B

重要

The turns ratio aaa applies directly to the Phase Voltages of the transformer windings, not blindly to the line voltages.

  • Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ) connection: Suitable for low voltage, high current (since IL=3IϕI_L = \sqrt{3} I_\phiIL​=3​Iϕ​).
  • Wye (Y\text{Y}Y) connection: Suitable for high voltage, low current (since VL=3VϕV_L = \sqrt{3} V_\phiVL​=3​Vϕ​).

§ Three-Phase Transformer Connections

A three-phase transformer bank can be connected in four ways:

1) Wye-Wye (Y-Y) Connection

  • The line voltage ratio is:

    VLPVLS=3VϕP3VϕS=a\frac{V_{LP}}{V_{LS}} = \frac{\sqrt{3} V_{\phi P}}{\sqrt{3} V_{\phi S}} = a VLS​VLP​​=3​VϕS​3​VϕP​​=a

注意

  1. If the loads are unbalanced, the neutral point will shift, causing severe unbalance in phase voltages.
  2. The third-harmonic voltage component can be very large.

重要

Why is the third-harmonic voltage large? The third-harmonic magnetizing currents in all three phases are in-phase (3(ωt−120∘)=3ωt3(\omega t - 120^\circ) = 3\omega t3(ωt−120∘)=3ωt). Being zero-sequence components, they require a return path to flow. In an ungrounded Y-Y\text{Y-Y}Y-Y connection, they cannot flow, distorting the core flux and inducing large third-harmonic voltages.

Solutions:

  1. Solidly ground the neutral of the primary winding to the source neutral, providing a path for the third-harmonic currents.
  2. Add a Δ\DeltaΔ-connected tertiary winding. The third-harmonic currents circulate inside the closed Δ\DeltaΔ loop, suppressing the harmonic voltage.

重要

Why Δ\DeltaΔ is special? With a Delta connection, we do not need a neutral line to release the third-harmonic current. Its physical loop construction allows third-harmonic currents to circulate and be confined within the loop.

2) Wye-Delta (Y-Δ\text{Y-}\DeltaY-Δ) Connection:

  • The line voltage ratio is:

    VLPVLS=3VϕPVϕS=3a\frac{V_{LP}}{V_{LS}} = \frac{\sqrt{3} V_{\phi P}}{V_{\phi S}} = \sqrt{3} a VLS​VLP​​=VϕS​3​VϕP​​=3​a

  • There is a 30∘30^\circ30∘ phase shift between primary and secondary sides. Typically, the secondary line voltage lags the primary line voltage by 30∘30^\circ30∘.
  • Because of the closed Delta winding, we do not have third-harmonic components in Wye-Delta.
  • In the United States, the standard convention is that the secondary voltage lags the primary voltage by 30∘30^\circ30∘.

3) Delta-Wye (Δ-Y\Delta\text{-Y}Δ-Y) Connection:

  • The line voltage ratio is:

    VLPVLS=VϕP3VϕS=a3\frac{V_{LP}}{V_{LS}} = \frac{V_{\phi P}}{\sqrt{3} V_{\phi S}} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}} VLS​VLP​​=3​VϕS​VϕP​​=3​a​

Delta-Wye Connection Applications

  • Common Applications:
    • Widely used for step-down distribution (transforming a 3-phase 3-wire line to a 3-phase 4-wire line, providing a neutral for single-phase loads).
    • Used to isolate the ground of the Wye side from the source ground on the Delta side.

Summary:

  • Δ-Y\Delta\text{-Y}Δ-Y: Common for step-down distribution. Low-voltage side is grounded Wye (3-phase 4-wire). High-voltage Delta isolates zero-sequence currents.
  • Y-Δ\text{Y-}\DeltaY-Δ: Common for step-up generation or interconnection. High-voltage side is grounded Wye. Protection & Reference

4) Delta-Delta (Δ-Δ\Delta\text{-}\DeltaΔ-Δ) Connection:

  • Line voltage ratio:

    VLPVLS=a\frac{V_{LP}}{V_{LS}} = a VLS​VLP​​=a

注

Δ-Δ\Delta\text{-}\DeltaΔ-Δ Connection is rarely used because it does not have a neutral line to provide necessary protection for operation.

§ Three-Phase Transformation Using Two Transformers

In emergencies or for low-power applications, three-phase power can be transformed using only two single-phase transformers.

1) V-V\text{V-V}V-V Connection (Open Delta):

If one transformer in a Δ-Δ\Delta\text{-}\DeltaΔ-Δ bank is removed, the remaining two can still supply a symmetrical three-phase voltage system to the load.

Power Rating of V-V Connection

Even if we remove one phase, the terminal line voltages VABV_{AB}VAB​, VBCV_{BC}VBC​, VCAV_{CA}VCA​ remain symmetrical.

  • Power capacity of V-V\text{V-V}V-V connection: The total active power delivered by two transformers is:

    P=3VLILcos⁡θP = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \cos\theta P=3​VL​IL​cosθ

    Since the line current ILI_LIL​ cannot exceed the rated phase current IϕI_\phiIϕ​ of the individual transformer, the apparent power capacity of the open-delta bank is:

    SV-V=3VϕIϕS_{\text{V-V}} = \sqrt{3} V_\phi I_\phi SV-V​=3​Vϕ​Iϕ​

    Comparing to a full Δ-Δ\Delta\text{-}\DeltaΔ-Δ bank (SΔ-Δ=3VϕIϕS_{\Delta\text{-}\Delta} = 3 V_\phi I_\phiSΔ-Δ​=3Vϕ​Iϕ​):

    SV-VSΔ-Δ=33≈0.577(57.7%)\frac{S_{\text{V-V}}}{S_{\Delta\text{-}\Delta}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 0.577 \quad (57.7\%) SΔ-Δ​SV-V​​=33​​≈0.577(57.7%)

    The bank can only deliver 57.7%57.7\%57.7% of the capacity of a three-transformer bank. Compared to the sum of the ratings of the two remaining transformers:

    SV-V2Sϕ=32≈0.866(86.6%)\frac{S_{\text{V-V}}}{2 S_\phi} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866 \quad (86.6\%) 2Sϕ​SV-V​​=23​​≈0.866(86.6%)

    Therefore, the transformers operate at 86.6%86.6\%86.6% of their combined capacity.

§ Open-Delta Phasor Relations

  • In the V-V\text{V-V}V-V connection, the phase currents are out of phase with their phase voltages by 30∘30^\circ30∘.

  • Power delivered by each transformer:

    P1=VϕIϕcos⁡(30∘−θ)P_1 = V_\phi I_\phi \cos(30^\circ - \theta) P1​=Vϕ​Iϕ​cos(30∘−θ)

    P2=VϕIϕcos⁡(30∘+θ)P_2 = V_\phi I_\phi \cos(30^\circ + \theta) P2​=Vϕ​Iϕ​cos(30∘+θ)

    • For a unity power factor load (θ=0∘\theta = 0^\circθ=0∘), one transformer operates at a lagging power factor of 0.8660.8660.866, and the other operates at a leading power factor of 0.8660.8660.866.

§ Open Wye - Open Delta and Scott-T Connections

2) Open Wye - Open Delta (Open Y\text{Y}Y - Open Δ\DeltaΔ) Connection:

  • The primary neutral line must be connected back to the source neutral.
  • Drawback: A large return current flows through the primary neutral line, which can cause significant unbalance and noise.

3) Scott-T Connection:

  • Used to convert three-phase power into two-phase power (and vice versa).
  • Common in electric railroad applications where heavy single-phase locomotive loads are balanced across a three-phase utility supply.

§ Scott-T and T-T Connections

The Scott-T connection uses two single-phase transformers:

  • A main transformer (connected across line BC, with a center tap).
  • A teaser transformer (connected between phase A and the main transformer center tap, having 86.6%86.6\%86.6% of the turns of the main transformer).

4) T-T Three-Phase Connection: Uses two T-connected transformers to perform 3-phase to 3-phase transformation. It is lighter and cheaper than a standard three-phase transformer bank.

§ Transformer Ratings and Related Problems

1. Voltage Rating:

  • Prevents over-voltage insulation breakdown.
  • Prevents core saturation. Since core flux is:

    ϕ(t)=1Np∫vp(t)dt\phi(t) = \frac{1}{N_p} \int v_p(t) dt ϕ(t)=Np​1​∫vp​(t)dt

    If voltage VmV_mVm​ is too high or frequency fff is too low, the core will saturate, causing massive magnetizing currents.

§ Frequency Limitation and Inrush Current

2. Frequency Limitation:

  • A 60 Hz60\text{ Hz}60 Hz transformer operated on 50 Hz50\text{ Hz}50 Hz requires the input voltage to be reduced by 20%20\%20% to prevent saturation.
  • A 50 Hz50\text{ Hz}50 Hz transformer operated on 60 Hz60\text{ Hz}60 Hz can handle up to 20%20\%20% higher voltage.

3. Inrush Current Problem:

  • When first turned on, the transient flux can reach up to 2ϕmax+ϕr2\phi_{max} + \phi_r2ϕmax​+ϕr​ (due to residual flux). This drives the core deep into saturation, resulting in a large magnetizing current spike (inrush current).

§ Parallel Operation of Transformers

Advantages of parallel operation:

  • Flexible operation facing load changes, improving overall efficiency.
  • Cost-effective (easier to replace or maintain smaller units).
  • Highly expandable for future capacity planning.

Ideal parallel operation conditions:

  • No circulating currents under no-load conditions.
  • Each unit shares the load in proportion to its power rating.

§ How to Achieve Parallel Operation

To achieve ideal parallel operation:

  1. Same voltage rating (turns ratio must be equal; difference should be <0.5%< 0.5\%<0.5%).
  2. Same phase angle shift between primary and secondary (same connection group).
  3. Short-circuit impedance (per-unit impedance) should be similar to ensure equal load sharing.

§ Load Sharing and Per-Unit System

Load sharing between parallel units:

IAIB=ZBZA\frac{I_A}{I_B} = \frac{Z_B}{Z_A} IB​IA​​=ZA​ZB​​

The Per-Unit (PU) System:

Per-Unit Value=Actual QuantityBase Quantity\text{Per-Unit Value} = \frac{\text{Actual Quantity}}{\text{Base Quantity}} Per-Unit Value=Base QuantityActual Quantity​

Base value relationships:

  • Pbase=Qbase=SbaseP_{base} = Q_{base} = S_{base}Pbase​=Qbase​=Sbase​
  • VbaseV_{base}Vbase​ is defined.
  • Ibase=SbaseVbaseI_{base} = \frac{S_{base}}{V_{base}}Ibase​=Vbase​Sbase​​
  • Zbase=Vbase2SbaseZ_{base} = \frac{V_{base}^2}{S_{base}}Zbase​=Sbase​Vbase2​​

§ Per-Unit System for Transformers

For transformers:

  • The rated apparent power SNS_NSN​ is used as SbaseS_{base}Sbase​.
  • The rated voltages of the primary and secondary windings are used as VbaseV_{base}Vbase​ on their respective sides.
  • Advantage: The per-unit system eliminates the turns ratio aaa from the equivalent circuit! The per-unit impedance remains the same whether calculated from the primary or secondary side:

    Zpu,p=Zpu,sZ_{pu,p} = Z_{pu,s} Zpu,p​=Zpu,s​

III. AC Machinery Fundamentals

AC machines can be divided into two major classes:

  • Synchronous machines: The magnetic field is generated by a rotor supplied with DC current (or permanent magnets), and the rotor rotates at synchronous speed.
  • Asynchronous (Induction) machines: The rotor magnetic field is induced by electromagnetic induction from the stator currents. The rotor always rotates slower than the synchronous speed.

§ Simple Loop in a Uniform Magnetic Field

To understand AC generators, we analyze a simple rotating loop in a uniform magnetic field:

According to Faraday's law of induced voltage on a moving wire:

eind=(v⃗×B⃗)⋅l⃗e_{ind} = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{l} eind​=(v×B)⋅l

For the rotating loop of radius rrr and length lll rotating at angular speed ω\omegaω:

  • Segment ab: The velocity vector v⃗\vec{v}v is directed at angle θ\thetaθ to the B⃗\vec{B}B field.

    eba=vBlsin⁡θab(directed into the page)e_{ba} = v B l \sin\theta_{ab} \quad (\text{directed into the page}) eba​=vBlsinθab​(directed into the page)

  • Segment cd:

    edc=vBlsin⁡θcd(directed out of the page)e_{dc} = v B l \sin\theta_{cd} \quad (\text{directed out of the page}) edc​=vBlsinθcd​(directed out of the page)

  • Segments bc and ad: Since the velocity is parallel to the magnetic field along these segments, the induced voltage is zero.

    ebc=ead=0e_{bc} = e_{ad} = 0 ebc​=ead​=0

The total induced voltage around the loop is:

eind=eba+edc=2vBlsin⁡θe_{ind} = e_{ba} + e_{dc} = 2 v B l \sin\theta eind​=eba​+edc​=2vBlsinθ

Using the relationships v=rωv = r \omegav=rω and the loop area A=2rlA = 2 r lA=2rl, we get:

eind=2rωBlsin⁡ωt=ABωsin⁡ωte_{ind} = 2 r \omega B l \sin\omega t = A B \omega \sin\omega t eind​=2rωBlsinωt=ABωsinωt

Since the maximum flux through the loop is Φmax=AB\Phi_{max} = A BΦmax​=AB, the induced voltage can be written as:

eind=Φmaxωsin⁡ωte_{ind} = \Phi_{max} \omega \sin\omega t eind​=Φmax​ωsinωt

§ Induced Torque in a Current-Carrying Loop

When the loop carries a current iii, a magnetic force is exerted on the wire segments:

F⃗=i(l⃗×B⃗)\vec{F} = i (\vec{l} \times \vec{B}) F=i(l×B)

The torque on each segment is:

τ=F⋅rsin⁡θ\tau = F \cdot r \sin\theta τ=F⋅rsinθ

  • Segment ab:

    τab=rilBsin⁡θab(clockwise)\tau_{ab} = r i l B \sin\theta_{ab} \quad (\text{clockwise}) τab​=rilBsinθab​(clockwise)

  • Segment cd:

    τcd=rilBsin⁡θcd(clockwise)\tau_{cd} = r i l B \sin\theta_{cd} \quad (\text{clockwise}) τcd​=rilBsinθcd​(clockwise)

  • Segments bc and ad: Induced torque is zero.

    τbc=τad=0\tau_{bc} = \tau_{ad} = 0 τbc​=τad​=0

The total induced torque is:

τind=2rilBsin⁡θ\tau_{ind} = 2 r i l B \sin\theta τind​=2rilBsinθ

This can be alternatively expressed in vector form using the loop's magnetic moment:

τ⃗ind=kB⃗R×B⃗S\vec{\tau}_{ind} = k \vec{B}_R \times \vec{B}_S τind​=kBR​×BS​

where B⃗R\vec{B}_RBR​ is the rotor-produced flux density and B⃗S\vec{B}_SBS​ is the stator-produced flux density.

§ Rotating Magnetic Field

In real AC machines, instead of a rotating loop in a stationary magnetic field, we have a rotating magnetic field (RMF) interacting with stationary windings (stator).

To generate a rotating magnetic field, we place three coils spaced 120∘120^\circ120∘ electrical degrees apart on the stator and supply them with balanced three-phase currents:

ia(t)=Imcos⁡ωti_a(t) = I_m \cos\omega t ia​(t)=Im​cosωt

ib(t)=Imcos⁡(ωt−120∘)i_b(t) = I_m \cos(\omega t - 120^\circ) ib​(t)=Im​cos(ωt−120∘)

ic(t)=Imcos⁡(ωt−240∘)i_c(t) = I_m \cos(\omega t - 240^\circ) ic​(t)=Im​cos(ωt−240∘)

  • Armature winding: Located on the stator, used to collect electrical power (generator) or supply power (motor).
  • Field winding: Located on the rotor, supplied with DC current to generate the main magnetic field.

§ Induced Voltage on a Three-Phase Stator

Assuming the rotor produces a sinusoidally distributed flux density:

B(θ)=Bmcos⁡θB(\theta) = B_m \cos\theta B(θ)=Bm​cosθ

As the rotor rotates at electrical speed ω\omegaω:

B(θ,t)=Bmcos⁡(ωt−θ)B(\theta, t) = B_m \cos(\omega t - \theta) B(θ,t)=Bm​cos(ωt−θ)

The total induced voltage in an NcN_cNc​-turn stator coil is:

eind(t)=NcΦmaxωsin⁡ωte_{ind}(t) = N_c \Phi_{max} \omega \sin\omega t eind​(t)=Nc​Φmax​ωsinωt

For three coils spaced 120∘120^\circ120∘ apart, the induced voltages are:

eaa′(t)=Emaxsin⁡ωte_{aa'}(t) = E_{max} \sin\omega t eaa′​(t)=Emax​sinωt

ebb′(t)=Emaxsin⁡(ωt−120∘)e_{bb'}(t) = E_{max} \sin(\omega t - 120^\circ) ebb′​(t)=Emax​sin(ωt−120∘)

ecc′(t)=Emaxsin⁡(ωt−240∘)e_{cc'}(t) = E_{max} \sin(\omega t - 240^\circ) ecc′​(t)=Emax​sin(ωt−240∘)

The RMS phase voltage is:

Erms=Emax2=NcΦmaxω2=2πfNcΦmax≈4.44fNcΦmaxE_{rms} = \frac{E_{max}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{N_c \Phi_{max} \omega}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} \pi f N_c \Phi_{max} \approx 4.44 f N_c \Phi_{max} Erms​=2​Emax​​=2​Nc​Φmax​ω​=2​πfNc​Φmax​≈4.44fNc​Φmax​

§ Three-Phase Stator Connections and Harmonics

  • Wye (Y) Connection:

    • Line-to-line voltage is VL=3VϕV_L = \sqrt{3} V_\phiVL​=3​Vϕ​.
    • The third-harmonic voltages (3ωt3\omega t3ωt, 3(ωt−120∘)=3ωt3(\omega t - 120^\circ) = 3\omega t3(ωt−120∘)=3ωt) in each phase are in-phase (zero-sequence). Because of this, the third harmonics cancel out in the line-to-line voltage:

      eAB,3=eA,3−eB,3=0e_{AB, 3} = e_{A, 3} - e_{B, 3} = 0 eAB,3​=eA,3​−eB,3​=0

    • Benefit: Line-to-line voltage contains no third-harmonic components.

  • Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ) Connection:

    • Line-to-line voltage equals phase voltage (VL=VϕV_L = V_\phiVL​=Vϕ​).
    • The third-harmonic voltages are in-phase and drive a circulating current around the closed Delta loop.
    • Benefit: No third-harmonic voltage exists at the terminals, but third-harmonic current circulates inside the Delta windings.

§ Distributed Winding and Breadth Factor

A simple concentrated winding produces a highly non-sinusoidal (square-like) air gap flux density containing significant odd harmonics:

B(θ)=Bs1+Bs3+Bs5+Bs7+…B(\theta) = B_{s1} + B_{s3} + B_{s5} + B_{s7} + \dots B(θ)=Bs1​+Bs3​+Bs5​+Bs7​+…

To make the flux density and induced voltage more sinusoidal, the windings are distributed across multiple slots.

  • Slot-pitch angle (lpha): The electrical angle between adjacent slots.

    α=p⋅360∘Q(electrical degrees)\alpha = \frac{p \cdot 360^\circ}{Q} \quad (\text{electrical degrees}) α=Qp⋅360∘​(electrical degrees)

  • Slots per pole per phase (qqq):

    q=Q2pmq = \frac{Q}{2pm} q=2pmQ​

    where QQQ is the total number of slots, ppp is the pole pairs, and mmm is the number of phases (m=3m=3m=3).

Breadth Factor (kdk_dkd​ or kbk_bkb​): Because the coils in adjacent slots are physically shifted by angle α\alphaα, their induced EMFs are out of phase. The vector sum of these EMFs is smaller than their algebraic sum. We define the breadth factor kdνk_{d\nu}kdν​ for the ν\nuν-th harmonic as:

kdν=sin⁡(qνα/2)qsin⁡(να/2)k_{d\nu} = \frac{\sin(q \nu \alpha / 2)}{q \sin(\nu \alpha / 2)} kdν​=qsin(να/2)sin(qνα/2)​

For the fundamental component (u=1 u = 1u=1):

kd1=sin⁡(qα/2)qsin⁡(α/2)k_{d1} = \frac{\sin(q \alpha / 2)}{q \sin(\alpha / 2)} kd1​=qsin(α/2)sin(qα/2)​

§ Double-Layer Winding and Pitch Factor

  • Double-layer winding: Each slot contains two coil sides (one top, one bottom), allowing the use of a fractional pitch (chorded winding).
  • Pitch ratio (yyy): The ratio of coil pitch to pole pitch (y=coil pitchτp≤1y = \frac{\text{coil pitch}}{\tau_p} \le 1y=τp​coil pitch​≤1). For a full-pitch coil, y=1y = 1y=1. For fractional pitch, y<1y < 1y<1.

Pitch Factor (kpk_pkp​): For a fractional-pitch coil, the coil sides are not exactly 180∘180^\circ180∘ electrical apart, reducing the induced EMF. The pitch factor kpνk_{p\nu}kpν​ for the ν\nuν-th harmonic is:

kpν=sin⁡(νyπ2)k_{p\nu} = \sin\left(\frac{\nu y \pi}{2}\right) kpν​=sin(2νyπ​)

  • Harmonic Elimination: By selecting a specific pitch ratio yyy, we can eliminate or significantly reduce certain harmonics:
    • To eliminate the 5th and 7th harmonics, we choose y=5/6≈0.83y = 5/6 \approx 0.83y=5/6≈0.83.
    • For y=5/6y = 5/6y=5/6, the fundamental pitch factor is kp1=sin⁡(5π/12)≈0.966k_{p1} = \sin(5\pi/12) \approx 0.966kp1​=sin(5π/12)≈0.966, while the 5th and 7th harmonic pitch factors are reduced to sin⁡(25π/12)≈0.259\sin(25\pi/12) \approx 0.259sin(25π/12)≈0.259 and sin⁡(35π/12)≈0.259\sin(35\pi/12) \approx 0.259sin(35π/12)≈0.259, successfully suppressing these harmonics.

§ Combined Winding Factor and Total EMF

The combined effect of distributed winding and fractional pitch is represented by the winding factor (kwk_wkw​):

kwν=kdν⋅kpνk_{w\nu} = k_{d\nu} \cdot k_{p\nu} kwν​=kdν​⋅kpν​

The total induced RMS EMF per phase for the fundamental component is:

E1=2πfNckw1Φ=4.44fNckw1ΦE_1 = \sqrt{2} \pi f N_c k_{w1} \Phi = 4.44 f N_c k_{w1} \Phi E1​=2​πfNc​kw1​Φ=4.44fNc​kw1​Φ

where NcN_cNc​ is the total number of series turns per phase:

Nc=2pqNKaN_c = \frac{2 p q N_K}{a} Nc​=a2pqNK​​

(NKN_KNK​: turns per coil, aaa: number of parallel paths).

For the ν\nuν-th harmonic:

Eν=4.44fNckwνΦνE_\nu = 4.44 f N_c k_{w\nu} \Phi_\nu Eν​=4.44fNc​kwν​Φν​

§ Armature MMF and Fourier Decomposition

When load currents flow through the stator armature windings, they generate an armature magnetomotive force (MMF).

For a single-phase winding carrying a sinusoidal current, the MMF is a pulsating standing wave:

f(x,t)=∑ν=1,3,5,…∞Fνcos⁡(νx)cos⁡(ωt)f(x, t) = \sum_{\nu=1,3,5,\dots}^{\infty} F_{\nu} \cos(\nu x) \cos(\omega t) f(x,t)=ν=1,3,5,…∑∞​Fν​cos(νx)cos(ωt)

where the peak MMF of the ν\nuν-th harmonic is:

Fν=4πNckwννImF_{\nu} = \frac{4}{\pi} \frac{N_c k_{w\nu}}{\nu} I_m Fν​=π4​νNc​kwν​​Im​

This pulsating MMF can be decomposed into two counter-rotating fields (Forward and Backward rotating fields):

f(x,t)=12Fνcos⁡(νx−ωt)+12Fνcos⁡(νx+ωt)f(x, t) = \frac{1}{2} F_{\nu} \cos(\nu x - \omega t) + \frac{1}{2} F_{\nu} \cos(\nu x + \omega t) f(x,t)=21​Fν​cos(νx−ωt)+21​Fν​cos(νx+ωt)

§ Generation of rotating magnetic field

When balanced three-phase currents flow through three-phase distributed windings, the individual phase MMFs sum up:

ftot(x,t)=fa(x,t)+fb(x,t)+fc(x,t)f_{tot}(x, t) = f_a(x, t) + f_b(x, t) + f_c(x, t) ftot​(x,t)=fa​(x,t)+fb​(x,t)+fc​(x,t)

Summing the forward and backward components for all three phases:

  • The backward-rotating components cancel each other out to zero.
  • The forward-rotating components add up constructively.

The total MMF of the fundamental component is a purely rotating magnetic field of constant magnitude:

Ftot(x,t)=32F1cos⁡(x−ωt)=32(4πNckw1Im)cos⁡(x−ωt)F_{tot}(x, t) = \frac{3}{2} F_1 \cos(x - \omega t) = \frac{3}{2} \left(\frac{4}{\pi} N_c k_{w1} I_m\right) \cos(x - \omega t) Ftot​(x,t)=23​F1​cos(x−ωt)=23​(π4​Nc​kw1​Im​)cos(x−ωt)

Ftot(x,t)=1.35Nckw1Irmscos⁡(x−ωt)F_{tot}(x, t) = 1.35 N_c k_{w1} I_{rms} \cos(x - \omega t) Ftot​(x,t)=1.35Nc​kw1​Irms​cos(x−ωt)

§ Speed and Frequency of the Rotating Field

The relationship between the electrical frequency fef_efe​ of the stator currents and the mechanical rotational speed nmn_mnm​ (rpm) of the rotating magnetic field is:

fe=P⋅nm120=p⋅fmf_e = \frac{P \cdot n_m}{120} = p \cdot f_m fe​=120P⋅nm​​=p⋅fm​

where PPP is the number of poles (p=P/2p = P/2p=P/2 is the number of pole pairs), and nmn_mnm​ is the synchronous speed.

ns=120fePn_s = \frac{120 f_e}{P} ns​=P120fe​​

  • Reversing Rotation Direction: Swap any two of the three stator phase connections (e.g. swap phase B and C). This changes the phase sequence from A−B−CA-B-CA−B−C to A−C−BA-C-BA−C−B, reversing the direction of the rotating magnetic field.

§ Space Harmonics in the MMF

For the ν\nuν-th harmonic MMF:

  • 3rd harmonic: Since the currents are 120∘120^\circ120∘ out of phase in time, the sum of third-harmonic MMFs is zero. There is no rotating 3rd-harmonic MMF.
  • 5th harmonic: Decomposing the 5th harmonic shows that it forms a negative-sequence rotating field. It rotates in the opposite direction (backward) at 1/51/51/5 of the synchronous speed:

    n5=−ns5n_5 = -\frac{n_s}{5} n5​=−5ns​​

  • 7th harmonic: Forms a positive-sequence rotating field. It rotates in the same direction (forward) at 1/71/71/7 of the synchronous speed:

    n7=+ns7n_7 = +\frac{n_s}{7} n7​=+7ns​​

§ Induced Torque and Power Flow

The interaction between the stator-produced magnetic field B⃗S\vec{B}_SBS​ and the rotor-produced magnetic field B⃗R\vec{B}_RBR​ generates an electromagnetic torque:

τ⃗ind=kB⃗R×B⃗S\vec{\tau}_{ind} = k \vec{B}_R \times \vec{B}_S τind​=kBR​×BS​

τind=kBRBSsin⁡δ\tau_{ind} = k B_R B_S \sin\delta τind​=kBR​BS​sinδ

where δ\deltaδ is the power angle (torque angle) between the two fields.

Power Flow in AC Machines:

  • Losses:

    1. Stator copper loss (3-phase): PSCL=3IA2RAP_{SCL} = 3 I_A^2 R_APSCL​=3IA2​RA​
    2. Rotor copper loss: PRCL=IR2RRP_{RCL} = I_R^2 R_RPRCL​=IR2​RR​
    3. Core losses (PcoreP_{core}Pcore​): Hysteresis and eddy currents in the stator core.
    4. Mechanical losses: Friction and windage.
    5. Stray losses: Miscellaneous load losses.

  • Power Flow Diagrams:

    • Generator:

      Pin (Mechanical)→Pconv (Converted)→Pout (Electrical)P_{in} \text{ (Mechanical)} \to P_{conv} \text{ (Converted)} \to P_{out} \text{ (Electrical)} Pin​ (Mechanical)→Pconv​ (Converted)→Pout​ (Electrical)

      Pconv=τindωm=Pout+PSCL+PcoreP_{conv} = \tau_{ind} \omega_m = P_{out} + P_{SCL} + P_{core} Pconv​=τind​ωm​=Pout​+PSCL​+Pcore​

    • Motor:

      Pin (Electrical)→Pconv (Converted)→Pout (Mechanical)P_{in} \text{ (Electrical)} \to P_{conv} \text{ (Converted)} \to P_{out} \text{ (Mechanical)} Pin​ (Electrical)→Pconv​ (Converted)→Pout​ (Mechanical)

      Pconv=Pin−PSCL−Pcore=τindωmP_{conv} = P_{in} - P_{SCL} - P_{core} = \tau_{ind} \omega_m Pconv​=Pin​−PSCL​−Pcore​=τind​ωm​

IV. Synchronous Machines

§ Synchronous Generator Construction

Synchronous generators (also called alternators) convert mechanical power into three-phase electrical power. Their construction consists of two main parts:

  • Field windings: Located on the rotor, supplied with DC current to produce the main magnetic field.
  • Armature windings: Located on the stator, where three-phase AC voltages are induced.

There are two rotor types:

  1. Salient-pole rotor: Large diameter and short axial length, with poles projecting outward from the rotor core. Used in low-speed applications (such as hydro-turbines).
  2. Non-salient pole (cylindrical) rotor: Small diameter and long axial length, with field windings embedded in slots. Used in high-speed applications (such as steam or gas turbines).

The speed of rotation of a synchronous generator nmn_mnm​ (in RPM) is directly locked to the electrical frequency fef_efe​:

fe=Pnm120f_e = \frac{P n_m}{120} fe​=120Pnm​​

where PPP is the number of poles.

§ Armature Reaction

When a synchronous generator operates under no-load conditions, the rotor field current IfI_fIf​ produces a rotor magnetic field B0B_0B0​ (associated with field MMF FfF_fFf​), which rotates at synchronous speed and induces a three-phase voltage in the stator windings.

Under load, three-phase currents flow through the stator windings, producing their own rotating stator magnetic field BaB_aBa​ (associated with armature MMF FaF_aFa​). The distortion of the net air-gap magnetic field by stator currents is called armature reaction.

§ No-Load Characteristics

On a per-phase basis, the induced no-load EMF E0E_0E0​ is given by:

E0=2πfeNckwΦ1=4.44feNckwΦ1E_0 = \sqrt{2} \pi f_e N_c k_w \Phi_1 = 4.44 f_e N_c k_w \Phi_1 E0​=2​πfe​Nc​kw​Φ1​=4.44fe​Nc​kw​Φ1​

where:

  • NcN_cNc​: number of series turns per phase
  • kwk_wkw​: winding factor (kw=kdkpk_w = k_d k_pkw​=kd​kp​)
  • Φ1\Phi_1Φ1​: fundamental flux per pole

Since Φ1∝Ff∝If\Phi_1 \propto F_f \propto I_fΦ1​∝Ff​∝If​, the induced EMF E0E_0E0​ is proportional to the field current IfI_fIf​ at low values. As the field current increases, the magnetic core begins to saturate, and the curve flattens. This is the Open-Circuit Characteristic (OCC).

§ Equivalent Circuit of a Synchronous Generator

To model the generator electrically under load, we assume linear magnetic conditions (neglecting saturation). Under this assumption, the net air-gap flux density BnetB_{net}Bnet​ is the vector sum of the rotor field BfB_fBf​ and the armature reaction field BaB_aBa​:

B⃗net=B⃗f+B⃗a\vec{B}_{net} = \vec{B}_f + \vec{B}_a Bnet​=Bf​+Ba​

Correspondingly, the net induced voltage E⃗s\vec{E}_sEs​ in the stator is:

E⃗s=E⃗0+E⃗a\vec{E}_s = \vec{E}_0 + \vec{E}_a Es​=E0​+Ea​

Since the armature reaction field B⃗a\vec{B}_aBa​ is produced by the armature current I⃗\vec{I}I, the induced EMF E⃗a\vec{E}_aEa​ lags the armature current I⃗\vec{I}I by 90∘90^\circ90∘. We can represent this relationship using an armature reaction reactance XaX_aXa​:

E⃗a=−jI⃗Xa\vec{E}_a = -j \vec{I} X_a Ea​=−jIXa​

Including the stator armature leakage reactance XlX_lXl​ and winding resistance RAR_ARA​, the terminal voltage V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​ is:

V⃗ϕ=E⃗s−jI⃗Xl−I⃗RA=E⃗0−jI⃗Xa−jI⃗Xl−I⃗RA\vec{V}_\phi = \vec{E}_s - j\vec{I}X_l - \vec{I}R_A = \vec{E}_0 - j\vec{I}X_a - j\vec{I}X_l - \vec{I}R_A Vϕ​=Es​−jIXl​−IRA​=E0​−jIXa​−jIXl​−IRA​

We define the total synchronous reactance as Xs=Xa+XlX_s = X_a + X_lXs​=Xa​+Xl​. Thus:

E⃗0=V⃗ϕ+I⃗RA+jI⃗Xs\vec{E}_0 = \vec{V}_\phi + \vec{I}R_A + j\vec{I}X_s E0​=Vϕ​+IRA​+jIXs​

The per-phase equivalent circuit of a synchronous generator consists of:

  1. Rotor field circuit (DC): Excitation voltage VFV_FVF​ supplying the field winding RFR_FRF​ and adjustable resistance RadjR_{adj}Radj​.
  2. Stator armature circuit (AC): The internal generated voltage E0E_0E0​ in series with RAR_ARA​ and jXsjX_sjXs​ supplying the phase terminal voltage VϕV_\phiVϕ​.

§ Phasor Diagram and Armature Reaction States

The angle ψ\psiψ is defined as the phase angle between the stator current I⃗\vec{I}I and the excitation EMF E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​. This angle determines the nature of the armature reaction:

  1. Cross-magnetizing armature reaction (ψ=0∘\psi = 0^\circψ=0∘): The stator current I⃗\vec{I}I is in phase with E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​. The armature MMF F⃗a\vec{F}_aFa​ lies along the q-axis, perpendicular to the field MMF F⃗f\vec{F}_fFf​ (d-axis). It distorts the field but does not demagnetize or magnetize it.
  2. Demagnetizing armature reaction (ψ=90∘\psi = 90^\circψ=90∘): The stator current I⃗\vec{I}I lags E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​ by 90∘90^\circ90∘ (purely inductive load). The armature MMF F⃗a\vec{F}_aFa​ directly opposes the field MMF F⃗f\vec{F}_fFf​ along the d-axis, reducing the net flux.
  3. Magnetizing armature reaction (ψ=−90∘\psi = -90^\circψ=−90∘): The stator current I⃗\vec{I}I leads E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​ by 90∘90^\circ90∘ (purely capacitive load). The armature MMF F⃗a\vec{F}_aFa​ aids the field MMF F⃗f\vec{F}_fFf​ along the d-axis, increasing the net flux.

§ Salient-Pole Machines and Two-Reaction Theory

In salient-pole machines, the air-gap length is highly non-uniform. The reluctance along the pole axis (d-axis) is much smaller than the reluctance along the interpolar axis (q-axis). Therefore, the armature reaction cannot be described by a single synchronous reactance XsX_sXs​.

Using two-reaction theory, we resolve the armature MMF F⃗a\vec{F}_aFa​ and current I⃗\vec{I}I into direct-axis (d-axis) and quadrature-axis (q-axis) components:

I⃗=I⃗d+I⃗q\vec{I} = \vec{I}_d + \vec{I}_q I=Id​+Iq​

Id=Isin⁡ψ,Iq=Icos⁡ψI_d = I \sin\psi, \quad I_q = I \cos\psi Id​=Isinψ,Iq​=Icosψ

The corresponding reactances are the d-axis synchronous reactance XdX_dXd​ and q-axis synchronous reactance XqX_qXq​:

Xd=Xl+XadX_d = X_l + X_{ad} Xd​=Xl​+Xad​

Xq=Xl+XaqX_q = X_l + X_{aq} Xq​=Xl​+Xaq​

Since the d-axis reluctance is smaller, the d-axis permeance is higher, meaning:

Xad>Xaq  ⟹  Xd>XqX_{ad} > X_{aq} \implies X_d > X_q Xad​>Xaq​⟹Xd​>Xq​

The excitation EMF E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​ is given by:

E⃗0=V⃗ϕ+I⃗RA+jI⃗dXd+jI⃗qXq\vec{E}_0 = \vec{V}_\phi + \vec{I}R_A + j\vec{I}_d X_d + j\vec{I}_q X_q E0​=Vϕ​+IRA​+jId​Xd​+jIq​Xq​

§ Phasor Diagram of Salient-Pole Generator

To draw the phasor diagram, we locate the d-axis and q-axis. The power angle δ\deltaδ is the angle between E⃗0\vec{E}_0E0​ and V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​, and ψ=δ+ϕ\psi = \delta + \phiψ=δ+ϕ, where ϕ\phiϕ is the power factor angle of the load.

Neglecting the armature resistance RAR_ARA​, the power angle δ\deltaδ can be calculated from:

tan⁡δ=IXqcos⁡ϕVϕ+IXqsin⁡ϕ\tan\delta = \frac{I X_q \cos\phi}{V_\phi + I X_q \sin\phi} tanδ=Vϕ​+IXq​sinϕIXq​cosϕ​

Once δ\deltaδ is found, we decompose the current:

Id=Isin⁡(δ+ϕ)I_d = I \sin(\delta + \phi) Id​=Isin(δ+ϕ)

Iq=Icos⁡(δ+ϕ)I_q = I \cos(\delta + \phi) Iq​=Icos(δ+ϕ)

The magnitude of the excitation EMF is:

E0=Vϕcos⁡δ+IdXd+IqRAE_0 = V_\phi \cos\delta + I_d X_d + I_q R_A E0​=Vϕ​cosδ+Id​Xd​+Iq​RA​

§ Open-Circuit and Short-Circuit Tests

The parameters RAR_ARA​ and XsX_sXs​ of a synchronous generator can be determined by two tests:

  1. Open-Circuit Test (OCC): The generator is driven at rated speed with open armature terminals. The field current IfI_fIf​ is varied, and the terminal voltage Voc=E0V_{oc} = E_0Voc​=E0​ is measured.
  2. Short-Circuit Test (SCC): The armature terminals are short-circuited. The field current IfI_fIf​ is increased from zero, and the armature current Isc=IAI_{sc} = I_AIsc​=IA​ is measured.
  • Why the SCC is a straight line: Under short-circuit, the impedance is dominated by the synchronous reactance (Xs≫RAX_s \gg R_AXs​≫RA​). The load is almost purely inductive (ψ≈90∘\psi \approx 90^\circψ≈90∘). The armature reaction is strongly demagnetizing, meaning the net MMF Fnet=Ff−FaF_{net} = F_f - F_aFnet​=Ff​−Fa​ is very small, keeping the machine far from saturation.

The synchronous impedance ZsZ_sZs​ is calculated at a given field current:

Zs=RA2+Xs2=E0 (from OCC)Isc (from SCC)Z_s = \sqrt{R_A^2 + X_s^2} = \frac{E_0 \text{ (from OCC)}}{I_{sc} \text{ (from SCC)}} Zs​=RA2​+Xs2​​=Isc​ (from SCC)E0​ (from OCC)​

Since Xs≫RAX_s \gg R_AXs​≫RA​, we have Xs≈ZsX_s \approx Z_sXs​≈Zs​.

The Short-Circuit Ratio (SCR) is defined as:

SCR=If,oc(VN)If,sc(IN)\text{SCR} = \frac{I_{f,oc} (V_N)}{I_{f,sc} (I_N)} SCR=If,sc​(IN​)If,oc​(VN​)​

SCR is the reciprocal of the per-unit synchronous reactance:

SCR=1Xs,pu\text{SCR} = \frac{1}{X_{s,pu}} SCR=Xs,pu​1​

§ Slip Test for Measuring Xd and Xq

In salient-pole machines, XdX_dXd​ and XqX_qXq​ are measured using a slip test:

  1. The field winding is open-circuited (If=0I_f = 0If​=0).
  2. A balanced three-phase voltage at reduced magnitude is applied to the armature windings.
  3. The rotor is driven by a prime mover at a speed slightly different from the synchronous speed (a very small slip).

As the stator MMF slowly slips past the rotor poles:

  • When the stator MMF aligns with the rotor d-axis, the reluctance is minimum, flux is maximum, current is minimum (IminI_{min}Imin​), and voltage is maximum (VmaxV_{max}Vmax​).
  • When the stator MMF aligns with the rotor q-axis, the reluctance is maximum, flux is minimum, current is maximum (ImaxI_{max}Imax​), and voltage is minimum (VminV_{min}Vmin​).

The reactances are calculated as:

Xd=Vmax3IminX_d = \frac{V_{max}}{\sqrt{3} I_{min}} Xd​=3​Imin​Vmax​​

Xq=Vmin3ImaxX_q = \frac{V_{min}}{\sqrt{3} I_{max}} Xq​=3​Imax​Vmin​​

§ Zero-Power-Factor Test and Potier Triangle

To determine the leakage reactance XlX_lXl​ and separate it from the armature reaction, a zero-power-factor (ZPF) test is conducted:

  1. The generator is loaded with an adjustable purely inductive load (power factor cos⁡ϕ=0\cos\phi = 0cosϕ=0 lagging).
  2. The field current IfI_fIf​ is adjusted while maintaining the armature current at its rated value INI_NIN​.
  3. The terminal voltage VVV is recorded for various values of IfI_fIf​. This yields the ZPF characteristic.

Using the Potier Triangle, we can determine the Potier reactance XpX_pXp​ (which is close to XlX_lXl​) and the demagnetizing armature reaction MMF FaF_aFa​.

§ Voltage Regulation of a Synchronous Generator

Voltage regulation (VR) is the percentage change in terminal voltage when rated load is removed:

VR=E0−VV×100%\text{VR} = \frac{E_0 - V}{V} \times 100\% VR=VE0​−V​×100%

  • Lagging PF (inductive load): I⃗\vec{I}I lags V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​. The armature reaction is demagnetizing, causing terminal voltage to drop sharply as load increases. VR is positive and large.
  • Unity PF (resistive load): I⃗\vec{I}I is in phase with V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​. Terminal voltage drops slightly. VR is positive and small.
  • Leading PF (capacitive load): I⃗\vec{I}I leads V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​. The armature reaction is magnetizing, causing terminal voltage to rise under load. VR can be negative.

§ External and Regulation Characteristics

The relationship between terminal voltage and load current (VTV_TVT​ vs IAI_AIA​) is the external characteristic. The relationship between field current and load current (IfI_fIf​ vs IAI_AIA​) required to keep terminal voltage constant is the regulation characteristic.

§ Power and Torque in a Synchronous Generator

Neglecting the armature resistance RAR_ARA​, the real power output PPP of a cylindrical rotor generator is:

P=3VϕEAXssin⁡δP = \frac{3 V_\phi E_A}{X_s} \sin\delta P=Xs​3Vϕ​EA​​sinδ

The induced torque τind\tau_{ind}τind​ is:

τind=Pωm=3VϕEAωmXssin⁡δ\tau_{ind} = \frac{P}{\omega_m} = \frac{3 V_\phi E_A}{\omega_m X_s} \sin\delta τind​=ωm​P​=ωm​Xs​3Vϕ​EA​​sinδ

The power angle δ\deltaδ is the electrical angle between E⃗A\vec{E}_AEA​ and V⃗ϕ\vec{V}_\phiVϕ​. The maximum output power occurs at δ=90∘\delta = 90^\circδ=90∘:

Pmax=3VϕEAXsP_{max} = \frac{3 V_\phi E_A}{X_s} Pmax​=Xs​3Vϕ​EA​​

§ Power Angle Characteristic of a Salient-Pole Machine

For a salient-pole machine, neglecting RAR_ARA​, the power is:

P=3VϕEAXdsin⁡δ+3Vϕ2(Xd−Xq)2XdXqsin⁡2δP = \frac{3 V_\phi E_A}{X_d} \sin\delta + \frac{3 V_\phi^2 (X_d - X_q)}{2 X_d X_q} \sin 2\delta P=Xd​3Vϕ​EA​​sinδ+2Xd​Xq​3Vϕ2​(Xd​−Xq​)​sin2δ

The power expression consists of two terms:

  1. Field excitation power: 3VϕEAXdsin⁡δ\frac{3 V_\phi E_A}{X_d} \sin\deltaXd​3Vϕ​EA​​sinδ (depends on rotor excitation EAE_AEA​).
  2. Reluctance power: 3Vϕ2(Xd−Xq)2XdXqsin⁡2δ\frac{3 V_\phi^2 (X_d - X_q)}{2 X_d X_q} \sin 2\delta2Xd​Xq​3Vϕ2​(Xd​−Xq​)​sin2δ (independent of excitation; exists because of the unequal inductances Xd≠XqX_d \neq X_qXd​=Xq​).

Due to the double-frequency reluctance component (sin⁡2δ\sin 2\deltasin2δ), the maximum power PmaxP_{max}Pmax​ of a salient-pole machine occurs at a power angle δ<90∘\delta < 90^\circδ<90∘.

§ Frequency-Power Characteristics of a Generator

The mechanical speed of a generator's prime mover is inversely proportional to the load power:

SD=nnl−nflnfl×100%\text{SD} = \frac{n_{nl} - n_{fl}}{n_{fl}} \times 100\% SD=nfl​nnl​−nfl​​×100%

The frequency-power relation is modeled as:

P=sp(fnl−fsys)P = s_p (f_{nl} - f_{sys}) P=sp​(fnl​−fsys​)

where:

  • fnlf_{nl}fnl​: no-load frequency of the generator
  • fsysf_{sys}fsys​: system frequency
  • sps_psp​: governor slope (kW/Hz)

§ Reactive Power and V-Curves of a Synchronous Machine

If a generator's active power output PPP is kept constant:

IAcos⁡ϕ=constantI_A \cos\phi = \text{constant} IA​cosϕ=constant

EAsin⁡δ=constantE_A \sin\delta = \text{constant} EA​sinδ=constant

As the excitation field current IfI_fIf​ is varied:

  • Normal excitation: cos⁡ϕ=1\cos\phi = 1cosϕ=1, the generator produces zero reactive power (Q=0Q = 0Q=0).
  • Overexcitation: The generator operates at a lagging power factor, supplying reactive power to the grid (Q>0Q > 0Q>0).
  • Underexcitation: The generator operates at a leading power factor, absorbing reactive power from the grid (Q<0Q < 0Q<0).

The plot of armature current IAI_AIA​ vs field current IfI_fIf​ forms a series of V-curves.

§ Parallel Operation of AC Generators

To connect a generator in parallel with an existing system, four conditions must be met:

  1. Voltage magnitudes: The RMS line voltages of the oncoming generator and the running system must be equal.
  2. Phase sequence: Both systems must have the same phase sequence (e.g., a−b−ca-b-ca−b−c).
  3. Phase angles: The phase angles of the two systems must be identical.
  4. Frequency: The frequency of the oncoming generator must be slightly higher than the system frequency to prevent it from acting as a motor immediately upon connection.

§ Parallel Operation with an Infinite Bus

When a generator is connected to an infinite bus:

  • The system frequency fsysf_{sys}fsys​ and terminal voltage VTV_TVT​ are fixed.
  • Adjusting the governor shifts the no-load frequency fnlf_{nl}fnl​, changing the active power output PPP of the generator:

    PG=sp(fnl−fsys)P_G = s_p (f_{nl} - f_{sys}) PG​=sp​(fnl​−fsys​)

  • Adjusting the field excitation IfI_fIf​ changes the reactive power output QQQ without affecting active power.

§ Power Sharing between Parallel Generators

When two generators of comparable size operate in parallel, the total active and reactive load must be shared between them:

Pload=PG1+PG2P_{load} = P_{G1} + P_{G2} Pload​=PG1​+PG2​

Qload=QG1+QG2Q_{load} = Q_{G1} + Q_{G2} Qload​=QG1​+QG2​

  • Adjusting the governor of one generator changes the active power allocation between them and alters the system frequency unless both governors are adjusted in opposite directions.
  • Adjusting the excitation of one generator changes the reactive power allocation between them and alters the terminal voltage.

§ House Diagram of a Parallel System

House diagrams show the frequency-power and voltage-reactive power relationships of two generators operating in parallel.

§ Synchronous Generator Transients

When a generator is synchronized to a grid, transients occur due to phase and speed differences:

  • If the generator speed is slightly faster before connection, a positive torque is induced:

    t⃗ind=kB⃗R×B⃗net\vec{t}_{ind} = k \vec{B}_R \times \vec{B}_{net} tind​=kBR​×Bnet​

    This torque acts as a mechanical load on the rotor, slowing it down to match the synchronous speed of the power grid.

§ Synchronous Generator Ratings

Synchronous machine ratings protect the windings and core from thermal and insulation breakdown:

  • Voltage and Frequency: Operating at lower frequencies (e.g. 50Hz for a 60Hz machine) requires reducing the rated voltage by the same proportion to prevent magnetic saturation.
  • Apparent Power: Limited by stator winding heating (IA2RAI_A^2 R_AIA2​RA​).

    Srated=3Vϕ,ratedIA,ratedS_{rated} = 3 V_{\phi,rated} I_{A,rated} Srated​=3Vϕ,rated​IA,rated​

  • Power Factor: Limited by field winding heating (If2RfI_f^2 R_fIf2​Rf​).

§ Generator Capability Curve

The capability curve describes the safe operating limits of a synchronous generator on a P-Q plane:

  1. Stator current limit: A circle centered at the origin with radius:

    S=3VϕIA,maxS = 3 V_\phi I_{A,max} S=3Vϕ​IA,max​

  2. Rotor current limit: A circle centered at (0,−3Vϕ2Xs)(0, -\frac{3 V_\phi^2}{X_s})(0,−Xs​3Vϕ2​​) with radius:

    3VϕEA,maxXs\frac{3 V_\phi E_{A,max}}{X_s} Xs​3Vϕ​EA,max​​

  3. Prime-mover power limit: A vertical line bounding active power output.

§ Synchronous Motor

A synchronous motor has the same physical structure as a generator but converts electrical power to mechanical power. At starting (nm=0n_m = 0nm​=0), the average torque is zero because the magnetic field rotates too quickly for the rotor to accelerate.

Methods to start a synchronous motor:

  1. Assisted start: Use an auxiliary prime mover (pony motor) to accelerate the rotor to synchronous speed before applying excitation.
  2. Variable frequency drive: Supply power at a low frequency and ramp it up as the motor accelerates.
  3. Amortisseur (damper) windings: Short-circuited bars in the pole faces act as an induction motor rotor during starting.

V. Induction Machines

§ Induction Motor Rotor Construction

Induction motors use a stator that produces a rotating magnetic field and a rotor that relies on electromagnetic induction. Rotor types:

  1. Squirrel-cage rotor: Consists of thick conducting bars laid in slots on the rotor core, short-circuited by end rings. It is simple, rugged, and requires no brushes.
  2. Wound rotor: Features a complete three-phase winding connected to slip rings and brushes. External resistors can be added to control starting current and torque.

§ Squirrel-Cage Rotor Equivalent Phases

The squirrel-cage rotor acts as a multi-phase system:

  • Number of phases mcm_cmc​ equals the number of rotor slots.
  • Winding factor kdp2=1k_{dp2} = 1kdp2​=1.
  • Stator rotating magnetic field speed:

    ns=120fePn_s = \frac{120 f_e}{P} ns​=P120fe​​

§ Principle of Operation

As the stator magnetic field rotates, it cuts the rotor bars and induces a voltage:

eind=(v⃗×B⃗)⋅l⃗e_{ind} = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{l} eind​=(v×B)⋅l

where v⃗\vec{v}v is the velocity of the bar relative to the magnetic field. The induced voltage drives a rotor current. Because of the rotor's leakage inductance, the rotor current lags behind the induced voltage. The interaction of the rotor current with the stator field produces torque:

τ⃗ind=kB⃗R×B⃗S\vec{\tau}_{ind} = k \vec{B}_R \times \vec{B}_S τind​=kBR​×BS​

This torque accelerates the rotor in the direction of the rotating field.

§ Slip and Mechanical Speed Relations

To induce voltage, the rotor mechanical speed nmn_mnm​ must be less than the synchronous speed nsn_sns​. We define the slip speed as nslip=ns−nmn_{slip} = n_s - n_mnslip​=ns​−nm​ and the slip sss as:

s=ns−nmns×100%s = \frac{n_s - n_m}{n_s} \times 100\% s=ns​ns​−nm​​×100%

  • At standstill: s=1s = 1s=1 (100%100\%100%).
  • At synchronous speed: s=0s = 0s=0.

The mechanical speed is:

nm=(1−s)ns,ωm=(1−s)ωsn_m = (1-s) n_s, \quad \omega_m = (1-s) \omega_s nm​=(1−s)ns​,ωm​=(1−s)ωs​

Stator frequency fef_efe​ and rotor frequency frf_rfr​ are related by:

fr=sfef_r = s f_e fr​=sfe​

The rotor MMF rotates at synchronous speed nsn_sns​ relative to the stator:

nR,stator=nr+nm=sns+(1−s)ns=nsn_{R,stator} = n_r + n_m = s n_s + (1-s) n_s = n_s nR,stator​=nr​+nm​=sns​+(1−s)ns​=ns​

§ Induction Motor Circuit Model under Locked-Rotor Conditions

At standstill (s=1s=1s=1), the induction motor acts as a static transformer. The effective turns ratio is:

ke=N1kw1N2kw2k_e = \frac{N_1 k_{w1}}{N_2 k_{w2}} ke​=N2​kw2​N1​kw1​​

Stator and rotor voltages are related by kek_eke​. The magnetizing current I0I_0I0​ supplies the main flux and accounts for core losses.

I0=Ia+ImI_0 = I_a + I_m I0​=Ia​+Im​

§ Equivalent Circuit of an Induction Motor

The per-phase equivalent circuit of an induction motor at standstill is identical to that of a transformer:

V⃗1=I⃗1R1+jI⃗1X1+E⃗1\vec{V}_1 = \vec{I}_1 R_1 + j\vec{I}_1 X_1 + \vec{E}_1 V1​=I1​R1​+jI1​X1​+E1​

E⃗1=−jI⃗0Xm\vec{E}_1 = -j\vec{I}_0 X_m E1​=−jI0​Xm​

E⃗2=I⃗2R2+jI⃗2X2\vec{E}_2 = \vec{I}_2 R_2 + j\vec{I}_2 X_2 E2​=I2​R2​+jI2​X2​

where:

  • R1,X1R_1, X_1R1​,X1​: stator resistance and leakage reactance
  • R2,X2R_2, X_2R2​,X2​: rotor resistance and leakage reactance
  • XmX_mXm​: magnetizing reactance

§ Secondary to Primary Side Parameter Conversion

Rotor parameters are referred to the stator using the effective turns ratio kek_eke​ and current ratio kik_iki​:

ke=N1kw1N2kw2,ki=m1N1kw1m2N2kw2k_e = \frac{N_1 k_{w1}}{N_2 k_{w2}}, \quad k_i = \frac{m_1 N_1 k_{w1}}{m_2 N_2 k_{w2}} ke​=N2​kw2​N1​kw1​​,ki​=m2​N2​kw2​m1​N1​kw1​​

E2′=keE2=E1E_2' = k_e E_2 = E_1 E2′​=ke​E2​=E1​

I2′=I2kiI_2' = \frac{I_2}{k_i} I2′​=ki​I2​​

R2′=kekiR2R_2' = k_e k_i R_2 R2′​=ke​ki​R2​

X2′=kekiX2X_2' = k_e k_i X_2 X2′​=ke​ki​X2​

§ Equivalent Circuit under Rotating Conditions

When the rotor is rotating at slip sss:

  • The rotor induced EMF is E2s=sE2E_{2s} = s E_2E2s​=sE2​.
  • The rotor leakage reactance is X2s=sX2X_{2s} = s X_2X2s​=sX2​. The rotor current is:

I2=sE2R2+jsX2=E2R2s+jX2I_2 = \frac{s E_2}{R_2 + j s X_2} = \frac{E_2}{\frac{R_2}{s} + j X_2} I2​=R2​+jsX2​sE2​​=sR2​​+jX2​E2​​

Referring to the stator:

I2′=E1R2′s+jX2′I_2' = \frac{E_1}{\frac{R_2'}{s} + j X_2'} I2′​=sR2′​​+jX2′​E1​​

The slip-dependent resistance R2′s\frac{R_2'}{s}sR2′​​ is split into two parts:

R2′s=R2′+R2′1−ss\frac{R_2'}{s} = R_2' + R_2' \frac{1-s}{s} sR2′​​=R2′​+R2′​s1−s​

where:

  • R2′R_2'R2′​: represents rotor copper losses.
  • R2′1−ssR_2' \frac{1-s}{s}R2′​s1−s​: represents converted mechanical power.

§ Determining Circuit Model Parameters

Induction motor parameters are determined using three tests:

  1. DC Test: Measures stator resistance R1R_1R1​.
  2. No-Load Test: Motor runs unexcited and unloaded (s≈0s \approx 0s≈0). Input power equals stator copper loss plus rotational losses (core loss + friction/windage).

    Pin=3I12R1+ProtP_{in} = 3 I_1^2 R_1 + P_{rot} Pin​=3I12​R1​+Prot​

    Znl≈X1+XmZ_{nl} \approx X_1 + X_m Znl​≈X1​+Xm​

  3. Locked-Rotor Test: Rotor is locked (s=1s = 1s=1). A reduced frequency voltage is applied to determine leakage reactances and rotor resistance.

    RLR=R1+R2′=PLR3ILR2R_{LR} = R_1 + R_2' = \frac{P_{LR}}{3 I_{LR}^2} RLR​=R1​+R2′​=3ILR2​PLR​​

    XLR′=X1+X2′=ZLR2−RLR2X_{LR}' = X_1 + X_2' = \sqrt{Z_{LR}^2 - R_{LR}^2} XLR′​=X1​+X2′​=ZLR2​−RLR2​​

    Reactance at rated frequency:

    XLR=XLR′fratedftestX_{LR} = X_{LR}' \frac{f_{rated}}{f_{test}} XLR​=XLR′​ftest​frated​​

§ Power and Torque in Induction Motors

The input power is:

Pin=3VLILcos⁡θP_{in} = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \cos\theta Pin​=3​VL​IL​cosθ

Stator copper loss and core loss:

PSCL=3I12R1,Pcore=3E12GcP_{SCL} = 3 I_1^2 R_1, \quad P_{core} = 3 E_1^2 G_c PSCL​=3I12​R1​,Pcore​=3E12​Gc​

Air-gap power:

PAG=Pin−PSCL−Pcore=3I2′2R2′sP_{AG} = P_{in} - P_{SCL} - P_{core} = 3 I_2'^2 \frac{R_2'}{s} PAG​=Pin​−PSCL​−Pcore​=3I2′2​sR2′​​

Rotor copper loss:

PRCL=3I2′2R2′=sPAGP_{RCL} = 3 I_2'^2 R_2' = s P_{AG} PRCL​=3I2′2​R2′​=sPAG​

Converted power (mechanical):

Pconv=PAG−PRCL=3I2′2R2′1−ss=(1−s)PAGP_{conv} = P_{AG} - P_{RCL} = 3 I_2'^2 R_2' \frac{1-s}{s} = (1-s) P_{AG} Pconv​=PAG​−PRCL​=3I2′2​R2′​s1−s​=(1−s)PAG​

Induced torque:

τind=PAGωs\tau_{ind} = \frac{P_{AG}}{\omega_s} τind​=ωs​PAG​​

Output power:

Pout=Pconv−PF&W−PmiscP_{out} = P_{conv} - P_{F\&W} - P_{misc} Pout​=Pconv​−PF&W​−Pmisc​

The power ratios are:

PAG:PRCL:Pconv=1:s:(1−s)P_{AG} : P_{RCL} : P_{conv} = 1 : s : (1-s) PAG​:PRCL​:Pconv​=1:s:(1−s)

§ Torque-Speed Characteristics of an Induction Motor

The induced torque is:

τind=kBRBSsin⁡δ\tau_{ind} = k B_R B_S \sin\delta τind​=kBR​BS​sinδ

Neglecting stator impedance:

V⃗1≈E⃗1  ⟹  Bnet≈constant\vec{V}_1 \approx \vec{E}_1 \implies B_{net} \approx \text{constant} V1​≈E1​⟹Bnet​≈constant

The torque-speed curve is divided into:

  1. Low-slip region: s→0s \to 0s→0, R2/s≫X2R_2/s \gg X_2R2​/s≫X2​, rotor power factor ≈1\approx 1≈1, torque is linear with slip.
  2. Moderate-slip region: Rotor reactance sX2s X_2sX2​ becomes comparable to R2R_2R2​. Torque reaches a maximum (pullout torque).
  3. High-slip region: s→1s \to 1s→1. High current but low torque due to low power factor.

§ Derivation of the Torque-Speed Equation

Using Thevenin's theorem at the stator side:

V⃗TH=V⃗ϕjXmR1+j(X1+Xm)≈V⃗ϕXmX1+Xm\vec{V}_{TH} = \vec{V}_\phi \frac{j X_m}{R_1 + j(X_1 + X_m)} \approx \vec{V}_\phi \frac{X_m}{X_1 + X_m} VTH​=Vϕ​R1​+j(X1​+Xm​)jXm​​≈Vϕ​X1​+Xm​Xm​​

ZTH=RTH+jXTH=jXm(R1+jX1)R1+j(X1+Xm)Z_{TH} = R_{TH} + j X_{TH} = \frac{j X_m (R_1 + j X_1)}{R_1 + j(X_1 + X_m)} ZTH​=RTH​+jXTH​=R1​+j(X1​+Xm​)jXm​(R1​+jX1​)​

RTH≈R1(XmX1+Xm)2,XTH≈X1R_{TH} \approx R_1 \left(\frac{X_m}{X_1 + X_m}\right)^2, \quad X_{TH} \approx X_1 RTH​≈R1​(X1​+Xm​Xm​​)2,XTH​≈X1​

The rotor current is:

I2′=VTH(RTH+R2′s)2+(XTH+X2′)2I_2' = \frac{V_{TH}}{\sqrt{\left(R_{TH} + \frac{R_2'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_{TH} + X_2')^2}} I2′​=(RTH​+sR2′​​)2+(XTH​+X2′​)2​VTH​​

The induced torque is:

τind=3VTH2R2′sωs[(RTH+R2′s)2+(XTH+X2′)2]\tau_{ind} = \frac{3 V_{TH}^2 \frac{R_2'}{s}}{\omega_s \left[\left(R_{TH} + \frac{R_2'}{s}\right)^2 + (X_{TH} + X_2')^2\right]} τind​=ωs​[(RTH​+sR2′​​)2+(XTH​+X2′​)2]3VTH2​sR2′​​​

§ Maximum (Pullout) Torque

By impedance matching, maximum torque occurs at:

smax=R2′RTH2+(XTH+X2′)2s_{max} = \frac{R_2'}{\sqrt{R_{TH}^2 + (X_{TH} + X_2')^2}} smax​=RTH2​+(XTH​+X2′​)2​R2′​​

The maximum torque is:

τmax=3VTH22ωs[RTH+RTH2+(XTH+X2′)2]\tau_{max} = \frac{3 V_{TH}^2}{2 \omega_s \left[R_{TH} + \sqrt{R_{TH}^2 + (X_{TH} + X_2')^2}\right]} τmax​=2ωs​[RTH​+RTH2​+(XTH​+X2′​)2​]3VTH2​​

The maximum torque is independent of rotor resistance R2R_2R2​, but the slip at which it occurs is proportional to R2R_2R2​.

§ Control by Rotor Bar Structure and NEMA Classes

Wound-rotor motors can vary R2R_2R2​ using external resistors. For cage rotors, variable rotor resistance is achieved using:

  • Deep rotor bars: At starting, high rotor frequency (equal to stator frequency) causes current to crowd to the top of the bars (skin effect), increasing resistance. At running, low rotor frequency allows current to distribute evenly, reducing resistance.
  • Double-cage rotor: Has an outer cage of high resistance/low reactance and an inner cage of low resistance/high reactance.

NEMA Design Classes (A, B, C, D) represent different starting torque and current characteristics.

§ Speed Control of an Induction Motor

Methods for speed control:

  1. Changing line voltage: Torque is proportional to V2V^2V2. High slip operation results in high rotor losses and low efficiency. Limited speed range.
  2. Changing rotor resistance: Wound-rotor only. Simple but inefficient.
  3. Variable Voltage Variable Frequency (VVVF) control: To prevent saturation, the stator voltage is scaled with frequency (V∝fV \propto fV∝f). Above rated frequency, voltage is constant and torque limit decreases (τ∝1/f\tau \propto 1/fτ∝1/f).

§ Starting of Induction Motors

The starting current is very large (5 to 8 times rated) while the starting torque is modest. Methods to reduce starting current:

  • Reduced-voltage starting (using autotransformer or star-delta starter).
  • Deep rotor bars / double cage.
  • Rotor resistance (wound rotor).

VI. DC Machines

§ Basic Principles of DC Machines

DC machines rely on a rotating armature winding and a stationary field system.

  • Induced EMF:

    Ea=KaΦωmE_a = K_a \Phi \omega_m Ea​=Ka​Φωm​

  • Induced torque:

    τind=KaΦIa\tau_{ind} = K_a \Phi I_a τind​=Ka​ΦIa​

where:

  • Ka=pNcπaK_a = \frac{p N_c}{\pi a}Ka​=πapNc​​ (machine constant)
  • Φ\PhiΦ: flux per pole
  • IaI_aIa​: armature current
  • ωm\omega_mωm​: rotor speed (rad/s)

The commutator acts as a mechanical rectifier, converting the internal AC voltage of the armature coils to DC at the brushes.

§ Voltage Ripple and Commutator Segments

A simple loop generator produces a highly pulsating DC voltage. By adding more coils and commutator segments, the brushes always connect to the coil inducing the highest instantaneous EMF. This reduces the voltage ripple (harmonics), producing a smooth DC output.

§ Armature Windings of DC Machines

DC armature windings are closed-loop windings classified into:

  1. Lap Winding: The ends of each coil are connected to adjacent commutator segments. The number of parallel paths aaa equals the number of poles PPP (a=Pa = Pa=P). Used for high current, low voltage applications.
  2. Wave Winding: The coil ends are connected to segments spaced far apart. The number of parallel paths is always two (a=2a = 2a=2). Used for high voltage, low current applications.

§ Problems with Commutation

During commutation, the armature current in a coil must reverse direction. Because of the coil's inductance LLL, a self-induced EMF (reactance voltage) opposes this change:

v=Ldidtv = L \frac{di}{dt} v=Ldtdi​

With short commutation times, this induced voltage is large, causing sparking at the brushes.

§ Solutions to Commutation Problems

  1. Interpoles (commutating poles): Small auxiliary poles placed between main poles. They induce a voltage in the short-circuited coil that cancels the reactance voltage and assists commutation.
  2. Compensating windings: Windings placed in the main pole faces, connected in series with the armature, to cancel the cross-magnetizing armature reaction MMF.

§ Armature Reaction in DC Machines

Under no-load, the air-gap flux density B0B_0B0​ is symmetrical, and the magnetic neutral axis (MNA) is perpendicular to the main pole axis.

Under load, the armature current generates a cross-magnetizing MMF FaF_aFa​ (along the q-axis). This distorts the net flux density:

  1. Neutral axis shift: The MNA shifts in the direction of rotation for a generator, and in the opposite direction for a motor.
  2. Flux weakening: Due to saturation at the pole tips, the net flux per pole decreases, reducing the induced EMF EaE_aEa​.

§ Equivalent Circuit of a DC Machine

The equivalent circuit consists of:

  • Field circuit: Vf=IfRfV_f = I_f R_fVf​=If​Rf​
  • Armature circuit: Vt=Ea±IaRaV_t = E_a \pm I_a R_aVt​=Ea​±Ia​Ra​ (−-− for generator, +++ for motor).
  • Converted power: Pconv=EaIa=τindωmP_{conv} = E_a I_a = \tau_{ind} \omega_mPconv​=Ea​Ia​=τind​ωm​.

§ DC Machine Excitation Types

DC machines are classified by how the field winding is connected:

  1. Separately Excited: Field winding is supplied by an independent DC source.
  2. Shunt: Field winding is connected in parallel with the armature.
  3. Series: Field winding is connected in series with the armature.
  4. Compound: Has both shunt and series windings (can be cumulatively or differentially compounded).
